text: This is why I love having these two gens in my team ❤️ REACHY RAP BATTLE SHOWDOWN - AI.ENGINEER SINGAPORE Unveiled at ai.engineer in Singapore today (Thorsten Schaeff as promised 🤣) Hugging Face Pollen Robotics Reachy rap battle, powered by Google DeepMind, ElevenLabs and more... Along with my long time collaborator Dr Richard Savery we built a real-time AI rap battle system with two Reachy Mini robots. (1) The flow: A human drops a prompt spoken on the mic. Local speech-to-text transcribes the prompt on an Apple Silicon Mac using MLX Whisper. The text is sent to Google DeepMind Gemini, which writes alternating rap battle verses for two characters. Each battle verse is rendered with custom ElevenLabs voices. The system combines the voices into a stereo battle track, with one rapper on the left channel and the other on the right. At the same time, we generate a timing manifest that maps each rap turn to a specific robot animation. Cycling '74 Max/MSP handles playback and show control. Python handles AI generation, voice rendering, timing, OSC messages, and robot choreography. The two Reachy Mini robots connect over WiFi and USB. When the battle plays, each robot performs when its voice is rapping, while the other keeps a smaller beat-driven groove so both stay alive on stage. The robots’ movement is word-aware: emphasized words create stronger gestures, and each robot has its own animation personality. The system prewarms robot connections before playback so audio and motion start in sync. (2) the Stack: Max/MSP, Python, Gemini, ElevenLabs, MLX Whisper, OSC, Reachy Mini SDK, Apple Silicon. A small fun idea turned into a full AI performance pipeline: prompt in, rap battle out, two robots arguing on beat 😎 And as mentioned in the video, special thanks to 🥃 Agrim Singh and Sherry Jiang and the whole 65labs team for making ai.engineer Singapore happen, and for listening to my crazy ideas about setting up a Robot Playground for the Embodied AI track! A few battle highlights in the video!

"We are perhaps one of the most privileged generations to be living through a revolution."

That's how Singapore's Foreign Minister Vivian Balakrishnan closed his keynote at AIE Singapore where he shared how he built a personal AI agent on NanoClaw and what he's learned from it.

He calls his NanoClaw agent his "second brain for a diplomat", saying he doesn't dare turn it off. 

Why NanoClaw? He picked it for the security, the readable codebase, and the containerized architecture. 

He said it himself, "As a surgeon, I know things will go wrong. When they break, you want them to break within barriers." 

He talks to it through WhatsApp, and, on top of it all, there are no config files to wrestle with. The agent relies on the LLM itself to handle all the customization, which means every person running NanoClaw is essentially running their own bespoke system.

So what does he use it for? The use-cases seem endless: briefings on the 12 countries he's visiting this month, remembering the hundreds of people he meets along the way, and first drafts of speeches and parliamentary answers.

And with that, his three rules for AI:

1. You can outsource computation, memory, and dissemination. You cannot outsource personal understanding. And if you hold authority, you cannot delegate accountability.

2. The real value AI brings society won't come from frontier labs. It'll come when people who actually know their jobs (teachers, technicians, doctors, lawyers, even ministers) embrace AI and rebuild how they do the work.

3. The barriers to building this have collapsed. Anyone can assemble these tools today, but you must get your hands dirty and learn by doing.

Sure, frontier models grab the headlines, but the real future gets built one workflow at a time, by people who actually know their craft. And, today, getting started has never been more accessible.

We couldn't be prouder to be part of this revolution, and to power your second brain, Minister!

Check out Dr. Balakrishnan's full speech — linked in comments!

Just wrapped our first AI Engineer Singapore.👏 👏 
3 days at Capitol Singapore, hundreds of builders in the room.
A year ago, "more AI Engineers than ML engineers" was a forecast. Today, you could feel it on the floor.

At our booth, the most common question wasn't "what does your agent do?" It was "how do you verify it?" Conversations skipped the demo and went straight to traces, eval setups, error handling, how the agent verifies itself.🦾 
That's the exact standard of rigor we hold ourselves to at MiroMind: A deep research agent engineered not merely to appear correct, but to be provably right.

Shout out to 65labs for the room. And to the MiroMind crew at the booth all three days — long weekend, but entirely worth it! 🫡

text: ai engineer singapore just wrapped, and i still don’t think i’ve fully processed it - or recovered from the sleep deprivation. this was a labor of love from our organizing team. i’m still sitting with everything that happened, but i wanted to share a few moments that stayed with me most. speakers flying in from around the world - many of whom we’d only known through the internet - showing up for builders here in singapore. staying late after talks, talking to students, and genuinely wanting to help (some even sharing they're thinking of moving to singapore 👀 ) minister Vivian Balakrishnan showing what it looks like when a world leader doesn’t just get briefed on ai, but actually tinkers with the tools himself. that conversation alone has already sparked debate and reached millions online. students realizing the infrastructure and access are already here - made possible by individual people who chose to sponsor scholars - to show up and care enough to support the next generation. and across almost every session, the same thread kept emerging: ai is forcing us to think more deeply about what it actually means to be human. finally, the closing line hit me hard: “you are the scene.” i moved from silicon valley to singapore in 2018, and this place embraced me. over the past 8 years, i’ve seen how much talent exists here - often in ways that are quietly underestimated. for a long time, it felt heartbreaking to hear people talk about singapore tech as if the only path forward was to leave - for founders to move abroad, for funds to pull out, for ambitious people to believe the real opportunities existed somewhere else. this weekend reminded me how wrong that narrative is. speakers, sponsors, founders, researchers, and engineers flew in from around the world because they believe something important is happening here. the scene is already here - and it was sitting in that room. i see singapore as a forward-deployed nation - a place where frontier technology meets everyday people and companies faster than almost anywhere else in the world. we tell people learning to vibe code that it only takes one step. this weekend felt like a first step toward something much bigger. more reflections soon. for now: grateful, overwhelmed, and already thinking about what comes next. 🥃 Agrim Singh Nehal Agrawal Adlin Zainal Ivan Leo Kaspar Hidayat Brian C. Daren T. 🇸🇬 Yong Quan Tan

text: One of the most insightful conversations on AI I’ve heard recently came from Vivian Balakrishnan, Singapore’s Minister for Foreign Affairs. Not because it was technical. Because it was deeply practical. Dr. Balakrishnan spoke about using a personalized AI agent — his “second brain” — to manage the cognitive complexity of international diplomacy. -No hype. -No futuristic narrative. Just a leader openly explaining how AI is becoming part of his daily workflow and decision-making process. My Top 3 Learnings from this conversation: 1️⃣ AI adoption becomes real when it becomes personal The biggest shift is not organizations deploying AI platforms. It is individuals redesigning how they think, learn, prepare, and execute using AI in their own workflows. 2️⃣ The barrier to experimentation has collapsed You no longer need to be an engineer to build meaningful AI-enabled systems. Curiosity, iteration, and “learning by doing” are becoming more valuable than waiting for perfect enterprise transformation programs. 3️⃣ AI can augment capability — but not accountability This was perhaps the most important point. AI can synthesize information and accelerate execution, but judgment, context, ethics, and responsibility still remain deeply human. 💡 That balance may define the next generation of leadership.💡 The leaders who experiment personally with AI tools will likely understand this transformation far better than those who only discuss it strategically from a distance. Simple message. Powerful implications for the future of work and leadership. Video: https://lnkd.in/g38ctD8y

text: Singapore is NanoClaw-crazy! Just got back from an incredible 39 hours in Singapore! 🇸🇬 Had the honor of meeting with Singapore's Minister of Foreign Affairs, Dr. Vivian Balakrishnan to discuss the future of secure and democratized access to AI agents. Singapore's vision for responsible AI adoption is inspiring, and I'm grateful for the opportunity to be part of that conversation. 🎤 Followed the minister on stage at AI Engineer Singapore, where I spoke to 600+ AI engineers about the agent factory we built to review and test every pull request on NanoClaw, and how we do it securely. 🤖 To prove the security works, I invited the entire audience to chat with my personal agent. It's connected to my emails, calendar, and call notes. 300 people took me up on it. 12 booked coffee meetings with me through the agent, each one approved by me in real time. 🎙️ Recorded a podcast episode with Latent Space Podcast Singapore blew me away. The energy, the talent, the ambition. First time visiting and I already know I'll be back. Grateful to Sherry Jiang and the AI Engineer team for an incredible event, and to the Singapore tech community for the warm welcome. Big news coming very soon. Stay tuned. Claws up!! Incredible !! Exciting times ahead !

text:
The "AI Gold Rush" of simple prompting is officially dead. The era of Contextual Infrastructure has arrived.

Last week at AI Engineer Singapore, the late-night founder dinners, community mixers, and closed-door builder sessions made one thing abundantly clear:

The market has hit absolute fatigue with isolated AI tools and shiny point-solution wrappers. If your AI system can’t connect fragmented data, handle complex multi-step logic, and operate with deterministic accuracy, it’s just noise.

At Insight Genesis (IGAi), these conversations match exactly what AI should be building towards to. The real value in AI has migrated from generating content to correlating data into deep human insights.

Here are the 3 structural shifts every founder, builder, and enterprise operator needs to watch right now:

1. From Isolated Tools to Data Fabrics
Organizations don’t want another chatbot that reads a single PDF. They need systems that sit across completely disconnected silos—multimodal streams like real-time voice, video analytics, and behavioral data—and map out hidden patterns, intent, and decision-making. True utility means moving from an AI that answers questions to a system that predicts behavior.

2. Multi-Agent Systems & MCP Are the Backbone
To build systems that understand human nuance reliably, engineers are abandoning single-model prompts. Production-grade deployment requires specialized multi-agent loops—where an Ingestion Agent filters raw telemetry, an Analytics Agent models behavioral data, and an Auditor Agent checks the output for accuracy.

3. Privacy-First & Decentralized Ownership
For an AI to provide deeply personalized insights, it needs access to highly sensitive data (wellness, biometrics, daily habits). The massive consensus among APAC builders is that privacy-first infrastructure is the ultimate gatekeeper for enterprise rollout. This is driving the convergence of AI + Web3, allowing users to retain sovereignty over their data vectors while training local or edge-based models securely.

My takeaway:
- The barrier to entry for building raw software has collapsed to near zero, which means the value of generic AI tools has dropped to zero alongside it.
-The builders who win the next wave won't be the ones with the best prompt. They will be the ones building sovereign, multi-agent frameworks capable of securely binding fragmented personal data into actionable intelligence.

Huge respect to the organizers, researchers, and builders pushing the boundaries in Singapore. For those building AI in Singapore, we are just getting started. 

My question is this: What is the biggest bottleneck you're facing when moving AI from prototype to production-grade deployment? 

Share them in the comments below. 

#AIEngineer #AgenticWorkflows #InsightGenesis #IGAi #PrivacyFirstAI #Web3 #SingaporeTech

text: Wanted to extend a massive thanks to the 65labs and the AI Engineer team for bringing strong "Builder" energy to Singapore. It was energizing (and occasionally exhausting!) to be surrounded by developers, designers, and fellow tinkerers over the past week. Was nice seeing familiar faces, while also making new connections. Also equally cool running into people you normally hear on your favorite podcasts (like swyx of the Latent Space Podcast - please check it out if you haven't yet). While I'm under no illusions that Singapore is some kind of global AI epicenter, there were still many things I felt proud of. 1. Seeing our Foreign Minister openly share his NanoClaw set-up. I think that takes leadership, particularly in front of a discerning technical audience. AI is also becoming an increasingly politically sensitive topic, so you're bound to become a lightning rod of sorts. 2. Meeting Singaporean founders who are based globally, but still want to contribute locally. 3. Watching a group of people 𝗲𝘅𝗲𝗿𝗰𝗶𝘀𝗲 𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗻𝗰𝘆 in support of what they believe in, even without broad consensus support (Sherry Jiang Agrim Singh Rachael De Foe Ivan Leo Brian C. Daren T. and many more). Events like this help inspire people (young and old) to build closer to the frontier - even when the landscape looks unclear. In Singapore, we often wait to see what institutions, incumbents, or the broader market validates before deciding what is acceptable to pursue. That approach isn't without merit. It creates some stability and predictability. But it can also make it harder for unconventional folks, creatives, or early builders to experiment at the edges before the rest of society catches up. A lot of what makes Singapore work today came from earlier generations 𝗺𝗮𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗰𝗵𝗼𝗶𝗰𝗲𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘄𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝗻𝗼𝗻-𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘀𝗲𝗻𝘀𝘂𝘀, but eventually proved correct. --- • Building a container terminal before container demand was clear; • Moving the airport from Paya Lebar to Changi in anticipation of the jumbo jet; • Even how we 'exited' ourselves from Malaysia in 1965 [Go visit the excellent Albatross File exhibition at the National Library if you haven't] --- We're living in a world with fewer templates to follow. We need more people willing to make thoughtful, non-consensus bets to build the future. * +6 Good bumping into you! non-consensus bets are the way to go!!

Watching a group of people 𝗲𝘅𝗲𝗿𝗰𝗶𝘀𝗲 𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗻𝗰𝘆 in support of what they believe in, even without broad consensus support (Sherry Jiang Agrim Singh Rachael De Foe Ivan Leo Brian C. Daren T. and many more). Events like this help inspire people (young and old) to build closer to the frontier - even when the landscape looks unclear. In Singapore, we often wait to see what institutions, incumbents, or the broader market validates before deciding what is acceptable to pursue. That approach isn't without merit. It creates some stability and predictability. But it can also make it harder for unconventional folks, creatives, or early builders to experiment at the edges before the rest of society catches up. A lot of what makes Singapore work today came from earlier generations 𝗺𝗮𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗰𝗵𝗼𝗶𝗰𝗲𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘄𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝗻𝗼𝗻-𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘀𝗲𝗻𝘀𝘂𝘀, but eventually proved correct. --- • Building a container terminal before container demand was clear; • Moving the airport from Paya Lebar to Changi in anticipation of the jumbo jet; • Even how we 'exited' ourselves from Malaysia in 1965 [Go visit the excellent Albatross File exhibition at the National Library if you haven't] --- We're living in a world with fewer templates to follow. We need more people willing to make thoughtful, non-consensus bets to build the future.

* +6

Good bumping into you!

non-consensus bets are the way to go!!

text:
아는 것과 해보는 것의 차이 - Ralphthon@SG 참가 후기

지난주 싱가포르에서 열린 AI Engineer SG는 여러 이슈로 많은 주목을 받았습니다.
그중에서도 가장 인상 깊었던 순간은
싱가포르 외교부 장관 Dr. Vivian Balakrishnan의 AI Agent 활용 사례였습니다.

AI와 직접적인 연관이 크지 않아 보이는 정부 부처의 수장이
직접 AI Agent를 설치하고(심지어 Raspberry Pi에), 
실제 활용 경험을 공유했다는 점이 정말로 인상적이었습니다.

“좋다는 걸 안다”가 아니라
“직접 써봤다”는 이야기였기 때문입니다.

지난주는 저에게도 ‘아는 것’에서 ‘해보는 것’으로 넘어간 한 주였습니다.
Ralphthon@SG 참가를 통해서였습니다.

그동안 Ralph Loop를 통해
AI가 지속적으로 개발을 수행하고 결과물을 만들어낼 수 있다는 개념은 알고 있었습니다.

또 서울, 샌프란시스코에서는 Ralphthon이라는 해커톤을 통해
이 과정을 실제로 구현하고 공유하는 자리도 있다는 것을 알고 있었습니다.

싱가포르에 있어 이런 행사들에 참가가 어려웠던 상황에서
Ralphthon@SG가 개최된다는 소식을 들었고
이 행사 참가를 통해 Ralph Loop를 제대로 한번 써보자고 마음먹었습니다.
신청서 필터링 과정에서 꽤 많은 사전 탈락자가 있는 상황이었음에도 
Hogun Min님께서 작성해주신 신청서 덕분에 팀을 이루어 참가할 수 있었습니다.

행사 전날, Ralph Loop 관련 자료를 추가로 찾아보며 정리했고
당일 활용을 위해 GitHub에 전체 구조를 나름 체계적으로 구성해두었습니다.

행사 당일에는 서비스 아이디어를 구체화하고
Ralph Loop에서 사용할 ticket들을 보완했습니다.

또 하나의 시도로는,
심사위원들의 LinkedIn 정보를 기반으로 각자의 persona를 만들고
각 loop 단계의 마지막마다 평가를 받도록 설계했습니다.

오후 1시, Ralph Loop가 시작되었습니다.
저희는 세션 발표를 들으며
ticket이 완료될 때마다 업데이트되는 GitHub를 통해
개발이 진행되는 과정을 지켜보고 있었습니다.

그리고 약 한 시간 후, 저희의 Ralph Loop는 종료되었고
화면에는 하나의 서비스가 완성된 형태로 정리되어 있었습니다.
원하는 형태로, 제대로 작동하는 mvp가 말이죠.

낯선 경험이었습니다.
스마트폰으로 AI Agent를 하나씩 지휘하던 방식과는 달리,
잘 설계된 구조 위에서 AI들이 스스로 판단하고
“알아서” 결과를 만들어내고 있었습니다.

직접 해보기 전에는 이렇게 생각했습니다.
“어차피 완벽하게 설계하기 어렵다면,
그때 그때 AI에게 지시하는 게 더 낫지 않을까?”
하지만 실제 경험은 달랐습니다.

그때 그때의 지시는 계속해서 전체 프로젝트의 방향을 수정하게 만들고,
그 결과 프로젝트의 초기 방향성을 흐리게 만들었습니다.

반면 Ralph Loop는
초기 기획의 방향성을 유지하면서도
그 안에서 AI가 자율적으로 작업을 수행할 수 있도록 만들어주었습니다.

새로운 개발 방법론을 경험했습니다.
정확히 말하면
이미 알고 있던 방법을, 이제는 실제로 사용할 수 있게 되었습니다.

시도하고 경험하지 않았다면 그저 알고 있었던 방법론에 그쳤을 것입니다.
하지만 직접 써봤고 그 장점을 알았기에 
이제 저의 주요 개발 방법론의 하나가 될 것이라 생각합니다.

이런 좋은 경험의 기회를 만들어주신 Goobong Jeong, Jongho Daniel Park, Seokhee Lee 님과 관계자분들께 감사의 말씀 드립니다.
잘 짜여진 시스템과 참가자간의 활발한 소통이 가능한 환경에서
싱가포르의 다양한 개발자들과 교류할 수 있었습니다.

행사에서 발표도 해주셨음에도 인사를 못 드렸습니다. 만나 뵈면 꼭 감사의 말씀 전하고 싶었는데요... Yeachan Heo 님 OmX 정말 잘 쓰고 있어요! 
그리고, 음주자가 별로 없던 개발자 행사에서 함께 맥주를 마셔준 Daniel Duma, PhD께도 감사드립니다. 😀

text:
FutureCOO: The real cost of GenAI to Asia

The convergence of generative AI demand, data centre expansion, and sustainability pressures in Asia presents a complex strategic challenge. I am investigating the cost of escalating compute needs arising from the accelerating adoption of GenAI (and possibly Agentic AI) for Asia's business and the general public.
3 of the 6 questions to cover:
1. How should all parties - regulators, DC operators, and enterprises - measure and allocate accountability for the true lifecycle footprint of AI, from model training to inference, across our hybrid cloud and on-premise environments?
2. How will leaders of enterprise balance the immediate operational efficiency gains from GenAI against the significant upfront infrastructure costs and energy spikes required to deploy and run these models at scale?
3. What specific metrics and reduction targets should regulators set for water usage effectiveness (WUE), and how will these be enforced with colocation providers and internal design teams?

Interested parties, please message me directly.
CXOCIETY FutureCOO Clarise Goh Nigel Standley Perry Zhao Christine T. Carol C. Sukhpreet Kaur Allan Tan Melinda Ramo Baylon Eileen Yu #sustainability #AIESG #ESG #AIgovernance #savewater #savetheplanet Iris Leong Hui Ting O. Preeti Pilare

text:
From watching AI Engineer videos on YouTube to attending the first-ever AI Engineer conference in Asia, held in Singapore in person, I've come full circle. I got to meet a bunch of cool people from all sorts of backgrounds:
- Quants
- FAANG engineers
- Fintech bros
- YC devs
- AI research guys
- founders
and a whole bunch of cracked engineers.

A huge shoutout to 65labs btw, for organizing such an incredible event that was jam-packed with value across workshops, talks and networking events.

There were events spanning software, design and physical AI domains and as a guy who primarily only keeps up with software AI, it was honestly sick to see the demos and engineering demonstrated by the physical AI orgs. 

It was also equally as amazing to see the companies working at the edge of what's possible and pushing boundaries in the AI agents space like 
- agent infrastructure and tooling
- context and memory management
- sandboxing and isolating runtimes
- agent security and boundary enforcement
- harness engineering
- running agents reliably at scale
- agent evaluation, testing, continuous iterative improvement
and more. Btw I'm gonna be making a bigger write-up/blog soon sharing stuff from the event, so stay tuned for that. 

And if any of this interests you, then you should definitely check out the videos on YouTube and also follow thesw cool companies -> Arize AI, Daytona, Tusk, Resaro, Hyperspell, LlamaIndex, ego AI (YC W24), autoscientific, Sakana AI  

Big thanks to Yuriy Braterskyy, the bossman and CEO of Superagent for bringing me along for this one(that’s us in the first photo). 

If you chatted with me at the event or just interested in this space, feel free to connect and come say Hi👋 in my DMs. 

#AIESG #AIEngineerSingapore #AIEngineer #Singapore #Agents #Builders

text: Back home from AI Engineer SG here is the gossip. Gossip is not a good habit, so perhaps just themes I saw and heard? People are fed up with Claude Code rate limits and pricing. This has forced those to Cursor or Codex. And upon opening up Cursor discovering how stable and beautiful it is, after recent updates in 3 from Ryo Lu's team. There was always a crowd waiting to chat with Codex community leader Gabriel Chua. Anthropic appeared to be absent. Due to legit organisational prowess by my fellow cursor ambassadors 🥃 Agrim Singh, Brian C. and Sherry Jiang we got frequent emails about the side events. Some of these were as high-calibre as the main event. Roster was thick and each night had multiple packed side events. Plus Cursor build night. At the Zo Computer and Daytona events a variety of solo's and startups. As well as a big warning on how the unit economics of business have changed from Geoffrey Huntley. The closest I came to this quality in community demo events was HCMC AI Tinkerers. Daytona are offering what I think will be the best escape valve for production agents outside AWS. Plenty of things to dwell of for agents. every attendee got a free agents book from Mastra's founder Sam Bhagwat. I believe Daytona and Mastra framework are combination for prod agents. Zo Computer seem to have the best option now for delivering an agent to my colleagues or friends who are non-technical and for whom deployment/security would be impossible. Hermes has taken over. OpenClaw has really suffered in the eyes of the crowd due to stability issues with many complaining about endless troubleshooting and breaking changes. The room at AWS for ClawCon was still full with festival atmosphere so the claw phenomenon has a hardcore fanbase. Designers make great speakers. Probably because per their speech's AI has brought these people from different disciplines back or into the world of code as outlet for creativity. Design speakers like Josh Newton from Microsoft, Cursor's Ryo Lu, Magic Path's Sabina Cabrera got people excited more than infra. If you work in AI you need to get tickets for the Melbourne event coming up in June you will not be disappointed. Especially if you get your boss to pay for it. I had a massive toothache. Excellent summary! Anthropic - I too felt so as nobody talked about Claude sessions anywhere in their online posts (I couldn't attend the event). Is Anthropic too rich already to care about community?😀 Toothaches are the worst… I once got my tooth extracted on the second morning of a 2 day workshop I was running. Hope you get that resolved soon! And great to meet you here. Woww Keith didn't know you dropped by for HCM AI Tinkerers! Thx for the shoutout, Son Le and Edward Tran must be proud :'')

text:
Sharing some observations with my thoughts still racing a full two days after the first AI Engineer Singapore. As many have shared, we are lucky to have a minister who “gets it” as a builder and craftsman himself. His words: “Real value comes from adoption of AI tools by people who understand their work re-engineering their work.” For me, this was what the conference was about: the signals came not from the industry titans but from people who were figuring things out for themselves.

I saw a demo by Le Yi Khor where she used Claude to engineer a whole customer data platform with full identity resolution when their google sheets solution exceeded the cell limit. I attended a workshop where Pierre-Loic Doulcet from LlamaIndex shared all the failures and lessons learnt building SOTA RAG systems. At another by 13-person wearemighty, they showed how they integrated Posthog into their product with a lifecycle engagement platform to build a product flywheel for trysecretsauce[dot]ai.

Here’s what resonated most from the rest of it: 

In a sea of noise, developing your judgment and focus from first principles matters more than ever. This was at its most visceral in the design talks by Phil Hedayatnia, Sabina Cabrera, Annie L. and Josh Newton. But, purposeful, mindful choices permeated every talk about agent architecture and infrastructure as well. In a world where the barriers to building and shipping have collapsed, the relative cost of ownership have exploded. Vercel’s Jimmy Lai summed this up best “Be careful about what you decide to own… doesn't mean that you should ship less but it just means that we have to ship with more focus, build what should exist, make it understandable, make it reliable, make it safe. And stand on the foundations that you can trust.”

Quicker and more parallelized feedback mechanisms. There's been a surprising amount of consensus around the following: devtools that allow frictionless testing of multiple versions in the cloud; investing in the tough integration work to make customer insights and organisational context accessible to anyone on the team; crowdsourcing the evolution of your product by open-sourcing (whether within the company or publicly), and observing how people improvise. Having just read Creative Selection (Ken Kocienda), this pattern was immediately familiar.

Lastly, pause to consolidate and reflect. I asked swyx, the founder of AIE, what enabled him to see 2-3 years ahead - he said: writing, it's a form of thinking. I’ve been behind on long-form posts - glad I took time to bang this out - a couple more pieces to follow.

Huge shout-out to 🥃 Agrim Singh, Sherry Jiang, Kaspar Hidayat, Rachael De Foe, swyx ​, and the rest of the organizers and volunteers at the event. Thank you for bringing the frontier to Singapore, and for gathering the builders figuring it out.

text:
Last weekend I got the chance to attend AI Engineer Singapore!😁 

The room was packed with builders pushing the frontier, from robotics to reasoning models to the future of AI. What I loved most was how wide the conversations were, spanning software, design, and physical AI, and still feeling grounded in what it takes to ship.

Two talks stood out for me personally:

- 🎙️Boris Starkov from ElevenLabs broke down what actually makes a voice agent feel conversational, and it’s so much more than just a strong TTS model. Turn detection, speculative generation, interruption handling, and all the small details that make voice feel human were fascinating. Their new Speech Engine especially got me excited as someone building AHMA, a voice-first AI companion for caregivers in Singapore. It made me rethink what “natural” interaction can look like, and how much more seamless voice AI could become.

- 🤝Michelle Julia N. from Blue Labs gave a talk that really stayed with me. The core idea was that AI needs to treat relationship-building and immediate utility as co-equal goals, not a nice-to-have, but a core design requirement for any AI that works with people over time. When it comes to understanding users, capturing someone's emotional state in the moment matters far more than their static personality traits, something current models need improvements on.

Also, a huge thank you to Patrick T. for the Codex demo! Seeing the agent work through all the tasks in real time was quite impressive, and I appreciated the time to chat through how it all fits together.

Overall, it was inspiring to learn from so many companies shaping how AI gets built and used, like Cursor, Figma, Cerebras, Prime Intellect, Reactor, and many more. Each one is pushing a different edge of what’s possible. AI is moving fast, but days like this remind me that the most interesting work isn’t just about what models can do. How we design them to work with us is just as important.

text:
Just wrapped up a side event I hosted during AI Engineer Week Singapore!

800+ signups. We could only accept 400.

The concept for this event was a simple premise. Most people wait for the right moment to start something. We put together a room of people who didn't.

→ OpenAI ran a live Codex session with their team. Real workflows with real QnA

→ Willis Wee built Tech in Asia from a blog, took it through YC W15, sold it to SPH Media, stepped down after 16 years this March

→ Ying Cong Seah had a full GIC scholarship and a 6-year Wharton bond. He paid it back and built Glints from a Google Sheet with 38 people

→Jonathan Liem started at 14 and worked for a diplomat by moving overseas, working on 9-fig projects.

→ Pairie Koh was a Stanford fellow at 17 and is doing research at a YC AI company before most people pick a major. 

The conversations were incredibly honest about what the first version actually looked like. What nobody warned you about and what it costs to hand something you built over to someone else.

Thank you to Aspire OpenAI Singtel for holding this with us alongside the help of Thomas Jeng Tyler Ryu William Liu Alyssa Nicole Ng-Misialek!

I'm also launching a space for young and exited founders who are actually building. Invite only.

DM/comment if you want in.

text: Singapore is no longer an "emerging" AI ecosystem. This week made that very clear. We have the second-highest Claude usage per capita in the world, according to Anthropic's AI Usage Index. I just got back from my first AI Engineer Singapore. Now I get it. One thing Adriel Yong said stuck with me. I asked him, "Did you fly in from SF for this?" He replied, "Half of SF is actually here right now." But the moment that really stayed with me was hearing Dr Vivian Balakrishnan speak. He said, "𝐘𝐨𝐮 𝐜𝐚𝐧𝐧𝐨𝐭 𝐠𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐧 𝐚 𝐭𝐞𝐜𝐡𝐧𝐨𝐥𝐨𝐠𝐲 𝐭𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐲𝐨𝐮 𝐡𝐚𝐯𝐞 𝐨𝐧𝐥𝐲 𝐛𝐞𝐞𝐧 𝐛𝐫𝐢𝐞𝐟𝐞𝐝 𝐨𝐧." Then he showed what he'd built with a NanoClaw and a Raspberry Pi. Most people sit on the sidelines of new technology and wait to be told what it means. He was saying the opposite: get your hands dirty. Build with it. Break things. Understand the potential, the limits, and the risks from the inside. I remember looking around the room and thinking, "Wait, this is actually happening here." I'm also really grateful my CTO, Bladen Lam, flew in for the conference. We spend most of our time heads-down building. Being in the same room watching this unfold was something else. What made it even more special was hearing from people who had attended AIE in the US and Europe say that Singapore's version was one of the best they had been to. That made me weirdly emotional. Because not that long ago, it felt like there was barely an AI ecosystem here. Now half of SF is in town and the conversation is about us. And when 🥃 Agrim Singh closed with "𝐘𝐨𝐮 𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐬𝐜𝐞𝐧𝐞," I actually had tears in my eyes. Because it's true. Ecosystems do not magically appear. They are built by the people who keep showing up, hosting, connecting, supporting, and giving a damn before the rest of the world notices. Huge shoutout to 65labs, Sherry Jiang, 🥃 Agrim Singh, Rachael De Foe, Adlin Zainal Ivan LeoKaspar Hidayat and everyone who made this happen. Founder life makes it way too hard to catch up with people properly, so getting to see Le Yi Khor, Kyra Cheng Jiaying Phil HedayatniaAdriel Yong Adriel HoLouisa Ong Jeff PanU-Zyn C. Saad HamidGiovanni Casinelli Yoeven D KhemlaniSudharshan Raman Yuriy Braterskyy and so many friends in one place was such a gift. You are the scene. * +2 Meanwhile, Kevin Tan H.A. is still stuck in KL. So close, but yet, so far! 🇸🇬 Wei... taking over the pink I see... 😂 thank you so much for coming and bringing Bladen Lam it was nice to meet him!! such kind words makes me still emotional seeing it - together we can all make the singapore scene a great place to be in :) Missed you at AI Engineer Singapore! Love the shades of pink that brighten the scene. <3 🥹 definitely a special one - more to come! (ps. still waiting to get some hot pink swag!!) so much love for you 🧩 Serena Lam!! thank you for being in the room while sg tech history happened!!! <3 🧩 Serena Lam Dr Balakrishnan's line is the one I keep thinking about. "You cannot govern a technology you have only been briefed on." That applies so far beyond government. I build WordPress sites, 360+ of them across international clients, and the single biggest gap I see is between people who read about AI tools and people who actually break things trying to use them. The ones who have built with it, even badly at first, are making entirely different decisions than the ones still waiting for a summary deck. Most people want to be told what a technology means before they touch it. That instinct is exactly backwards. The part about the ecosystem not magically appearing, that's real. Communities like this look inevitable from the outside and look like stubborn, unglamorous effort from the inside. The people who kept showing up before it was cool are the reason half of SF was in Singapore this week. Was there a specific conversation or session that shifted something for you personally, beyond the Dr Balakrishnan moment? TL;DR: Singapore may be one of the first countries to open a serious public conversation around adding “nutrition labels” to AI products. That says a lot about the speed at which the government, companies, and individuals here are adapting to this new shift. It is also why Singapore has managed to remain such a strong case study across generations... Convergence Summit | 12 June 2026 coming up next for folks who still can’t get enough. Singapore really does feel like the converging point for frontier tech right now!!! 🧩 Serena. A clear sign of how fast AI ecosystems can shift when people actively build and participate instead of waiting on the sidelines. Strong signals like high usage numbers only show part of the picture. The real change happens when builders, founders, and leaders start treating the place as a working ground for ideas instead of just observation. When conversations move from theory to hands-on building, the speed of learning increases, and the ecosystem starts shaping itself through real action instead of reports. ✨

The real change happens when builders, founders, and leaders start treating the place as a working ground for ideas instead of just observation. text:
"You cannot govern a technology you have only been briefed on."

Dr Vivian Balakrishnan, Minister for Foreign Affairs of Singapore, delivered this line in the keynote at AI Engineer Singapore last week. It belongs on the wall of every CEO's office, right next to the one about not buying isolated AI on top of unfixed operations.

Reading a deck on what an AI agent can do tells a leader what the technology promises. On the other hand, sitting with operators on the floor, walking through where data fragments, where decisions stall, where capacity leaks: that tells a leader what the technology is actually for in this business.

Three takeaways from the keynote worth flagging for any leader building with AI right now:
1) The edge is deployment. If one person can assemble useful AI in evenings, an SME can build domain AI for logistics, law, healthcare. The differentiation is not capability, it is who actually ships.

2) The goal is democratisation. Putting AI in the hands of every operator, so they use it in the way that works best for their own work. Not a centralised AI function. A workflow-level rebuild, function by function.

3) The approach is decentralisation. Sector by sector, project by project, workflow by workflow. The opposite of a program-led transformation.

That is the entire reason the Embiggen Method starts with one week of Operational Audit on site, on the operator's own platform. Diagnosis before prescription. Real workflows, real cost, real numbers. Before any roadmap. Before any pilot.

The tools are here. The question is what we build with them. The leaders who answer that question well are the ones who have done their own work first.

#AIEngineerSingapore #LearnByDoing #AIOperations #EmbiggenMethod

text:
I had the privilege of sharing some of our work at AI Engineer Singapore this past week alongside many incredibly sharp builders.

It’s easy to look at frontier AI and assume the important work only happens inside the big labs. But more and more, the real understanding comes from people trying to deploy these systems into the real world — figuring out what breaks, what scales, and where the gaps still are.

That was what made the event exciting for me. People weren’t just talking about AI in theory. They were openly sharing the challenges, tradeoffs, and lessons from actually building.

It feels like a real shift is starting to happen in Singapore. There’s a growing energy around people pushing these systems forward together instead of figuring it out alone.

Huge thanks to the 65labs team, especially Sherry Jiang and 🥃 Agrim Singh, for bringing the community together.

text:
« On ne peut pas maîtriser une technologie dont on n’a reçu qu’une simple présentation. »

Le Dr Vivian Balakrishnan, ministre des Affaires étrangères de Singapour, a prononcé cette phrase lors du discours d’ouverture de la conférence AI Engineer Singapore la semaine dernière. Elle mériterait d’être affichée sur le mur du bureau de chaque PDG, juste à côté de celle qui recommande de ne pas acheter de solutions d’IA isolées pour venir s’ajouter à des opérations non optimisées.

Lire une présentation sur ce qu’un agent IA peut faire indique à un dirigeant ce que la technologie promet. En revanche, s’asseoir avec les opérateurs sur le terrain, parcourir les endroits où les données se fragmentent, où les décisions s’enlisent, où les capacités s’échappent : cela indique à un dirigeant à quoi sert réellement la technologie dans cette entreprise.

Trois points à retenir du discours d’ouverture qui méritent d’être soulignés pour tout dirigeant qui développe actuellement avec l’IA :
1) L'avantage, c'est le déploiement. Si une seule personne peut mettre en place une IA utile le soir, une PME peut développer une IA métier pour la logistique, le droit ou la santé. La différence ne réside pas dans les capacités, mais dans qui met réellement en œuvre.

2) L'objectif est la démocratisation. Mettre l'IA entre les mains de chaque opérateur, afin qu'il l'utilise de la manière la plus adaptée à son propre travail. Pas une fonction IA centralisée. Une refonte au niveau des flux de travail, fonction par fonction.

3) L'approche est la décentralisation. Secteur par secteur, projet par projet, flux de travail par flux de travail. C'est l'opposé d'une transformation pilotée par un programme.

C'est précisément pour cette raison que la méthode Embiggen commence par une semaine d'audit opérationnel sur site, sur la plateforme même de l'opérateur. Le diagnostic avant la prescription. Des flux de travail réels, des coûts réels, des chiffres réels. Avant toute feuille de route. Avant tout projet pilote.

Les outils sont là. La question est de savoir ce que nous en faisons. Les dirigeants qui répondent bien à cette question sont ceux qui ont d'abord fait le travail nécessaire.

#AIEngineerSingapore #LearnByDoing #AIOperations #EmbiggenMethod

text:
„Nie da się zarządzać technologią, o której otrzymało się jedynie ogólne informacje”.

Dr Vivian Balakrishnan, minister spraw zagranicznych Singapuru, wypowiedział te słowa podczas przemówienia inauguracyjnego na konferencji AI Engineer Singapore w zeszłym tygodniu. Powinny one znaleźć się na ścianie w gabinecie każdego dyrektora generalnego, tuż obok sentencji o tym, by nie kupować odizolowanych rozwiązań AI w oparciu o nieustabilizowane procesy operacyjne.

Przeczytanie prezentacji na temat możliwości agenta AI pokazuje liderowi, co ta technologia obiecuje. Z drugiej strony, spotkanie z operatorami na miejscu, prześledzenie, gdzie dochodzi do fragmentacji danych, gdzie decyzje utknęły w martwym punkcie, gdzie dochodzi do utraty wydajności – to pokazuje liderowi, do czego ta technologia faktycznie służy w tej branży.

Trzy wnioski z przemówienia, na które warto zwrócić uwagę każdemu liderowi wdrażającemu obecnie AI:
1) Kluczowe znaczenie ma wdrożenie. Jeśli jedna osoba potrafi stworzyć użyteczną sztuczną inteligencję wieczorami, małe i średnie przedsiębiorstwo może zbudować sztuczną inteligencję dla logistyki, prawa czy opieki zdrowotnej. Różnica nie polega na możliwościach, ale na tym, kto faktycznie realizuje projekt.

2) Celem jest demokratyzacja. Oddanie sztucznej inteligencji w ręce każdego operatora, aby mógł z niej korzystać w sposób najlepiej odpowiadający jego pracy. Nie chodzi o scentralizowaną funkcję sztucznej inteligencji. Chodzi o przebudowę na poziomie przepływu pracy, funkcja po funkcji.

3) Podejście opiera się na decentralizacji. Sektor po sektorze, projekt po projekcie, przepływ pracy po przepływie pracy. Jest to przeciwieństwo transformacji kierowanej przez program.

Właśnie dlatego metoda Embiggen rozpoczyna się od tygodniowego audytu operacyjnego przeprowadzanego na miejscu, na platformie samego operatora. Najpierw diagnoza, potem zalecenia. Rzeczywiste procesy, rzeczywiste koszty, rzeczywiste dane. Zanim powstanie jakikolwiek plan działania. Zanim rozpocznie się jakikolwiek projekt pilotażowy.

Narzędzia są już dostępne. Pytanie brzmi: co z nich stworzymy? Liderzy, którzy potrafią dobrze odpowiedzieć na to pytanie, to ci, którzy najpierw wykonali swoją pracę.

#AIEngineerSingapore #LearnByDoing #AIOperations #EmbiggenMethod

Jeśli jedna osoba potrafi stworzyć użyteczną sztuczną inteligencję wieczorami, małe i średnie przedsiębiorstwo może zbudować sztuczną inteligencję dla logistyki, prawa czy opieki zdrowotnej. Różnica nie polega na możliwościach, ale na tym, kto faktycznie realizuje projekt.

2) Celem jest demokratyzacja. Oddanie sztucznej inteligencji w ręce każdego operatora, aby mógł z niej korzystać w sposób najlepiej odpowiadający jego pracy. Nie chodzi o scentralizowaną funkcję sztucznej inteligencji. Chodzi o przebudowę na poziomie przepływu pracy, funkcja po funkcji.

3) Podejście opiera się na decentralizacji. Sektor po sektorze, projekt po projekcie, przepływ pracy po przepływie pracy. Jest to przeciwieństwo transformacji kierowanej przez program.

Właśnie dlatego metoda Embiggen rozpoczyna się od tygodniowego audytu operacyjnego przeprowadzanego na miejscu, na platformie samego operatora. Najpierw diagnoza, potem zalecenia. Rzeczywiste procesy, rzeczywiste koszty, rzeczywiste dane. Zanim powstanie jakikolwiek plan działania. Zanim rozpocznie się jakikolwiek projekt pilotażowy.

Narzędzia są już dostępne. Pytanie brzmi: co z nich stworzymy? Liderzy, którzy potrafią dobrze odpowiedzieć na to pytanie, to ci, którzy najpierw wykonali swoją pracę.

Built out of Duolingo frustration. An AI language tutor that video-calls you, recognises objects through your camera, and turns your real world into the curriculum.

A voice agent for elderly care in Singapore. Short, natural check-in calls that quietly monitor wellbeing and alert family on Telegram if anything seems off.

text:
NanoClaw's creator turned down a $20M buyout offer and raised $12M seed instead

Gavriel Cohen built NanoClaw on his couch as a secure, sandboxed alternative to OpenClaw for running AI agents without exposing credentials and services. Within six weeks of writing the first line of code he had a viral endorsement from Andrej Karpathy, a shoutout from Singapore's foreign minister calling it his second brain, 50 plus investor DMs, a $20 million acquisition offer, and a term sheet.

He turned down the acquisition. Then raised a $12 million oversubscribed seed led by Valley Capital Partners with Docker, Vercel, Monday.com, Slow Ventures, and Hugging Face CEO Clem Delangue among the participants.

The enterprise angle emerged organically. Early technical users at Amazon, Google, Meta, and others set up NanoClaw for themselves and kept getting asked by coworkers to help them do the same. NanoCo is now offering forward deployed engineers to roll it out at scale.

Open source projects that solve a real pain point, security in this case, compound fast.

#AI #OpenSource #AIAgents #Startups #Fundraising #NanoClaw #TechNews

text:
When a $20 M buyout is on the table, most founders say yes — these brothers said no.  

In just six weeks, Gavriel and Lazer Cohen turned a couch‑coded project into NanoClaw, a sandboxed AI‑agent platform that captured the attention of Andrej Karpathy, Singapore’s foreign minister and dozens of tech execs. After viral praise, they declined a six‑figure offer, then a $20 M acquisition, and instead closed a $12 M seed round led by Valley Capital with participation from Docker, Vercel, Monday.com, Slow Ventures and Hugging Face’s CEO Clem Delangue.  

The Cohen brothers chose to double‑down on community. By keeping NanoClaw open source, they unlocked exponential contributions, early enterprise pilots at Amazon, Google, Meta and others, and a new “forward‑deployed engineer” service that helps companies roll out secure AI agents at scale.  

My take: this is a clear signal that the next wave of AI infrastructure will be built on open, sandboxed foundations where community momentum fuels both innovation and revenue. It also shows that strategic patience can turn a fleeting buzz into a sustainable business model.  

Do you think more AI founders should prioritize community growth over early exits, or is the lure of a quick acquisition still the smarter play?  

#AI #OpenSource #StartupFunding #EnterpriseAI #TechInnovation #VentureCapital #FutureOfWork

text: I gave a talk at AI Engineer Singapore on evaluating creative AI models and combating the problem of "death by prompting." Only fitting to edit my video with Gemini Omni that Google DeepMind released yesterday (link to the full talk in the comments). text: The people who are getting the most out of AI have put in deliberate, intentional practice. 🎸 You don't get better by listening to more music. You get better by practising deliberately - until the mechanics disappear and what remains is creativity. Geoffrey Huntley shared this ponderoo at AI Engineer last weekend. It reminded me of the time I started learning the guitar and it reframes the whole conversation. Not fear or FOMO. Curiosity. How do I get better? Three days in Singapore. The surface area of this event is wide - engineers, founders, researchers, operators, people building across every layer of the stack. And everyone was genuinely excited. Not the performed excitement of a conference where people are working the room. I bumped into people I've known for ten years and hadn't reconnected with in as long. On the last day, I brought my 4 year old to see robots and meet grownups who are good at math and computers. My favourite moment of that day was when we played his new favourite song for a group at the Google DeepMind booth - a song he'd made with me, from a conversation with Gemini using Lyria. He was the end user sharing his joy back to the people who built the thing. We talk a lot in this industry about who we're building for. On Sunday, that person was standing next to me asking if the robot could come home with us while his pocket was filled with ChatGPT stickers and an Exa goat plushie in his arms. Collegial, fun, the kind of event you don't want to leave, kudos once again to 🥃 Agrim Singh Sherry Jiang and 65labs. Daria Soboleva Min Kim Zoe Li Boris Starkov Grégoire Lionnet Tomithy T. It reminded me of the time I started learning the guitar and it reframes the whole conversation. Not fear or FOMO. Curiosity. How do I get better? Three days in Singapore. The surface area of this event is wide - engineers, founders, researchers, operators, people building across every layer of the stack. And everyone was genuinely excited. Not the performed excitement of a conference where people are working the room. I bumped into people I've known for ten years and hadn't reconnected with in as long. On the last day, I brought my 4 year old to see robots and meet grownups who are good at math and computers. My favourite moment of that day was when we played his new favourite song for a group at the Google DeepMind booth - a song he'd made with me, from a conversation with Gemini using Lyria. He was the end user sharing his joy back to the people who built the thing. We talk a lot in this industry about who we're building for. text:
AI Engineer Singapore Recap: Worth reading. Also worth pushing back on.

I've got five takes. Here's where I agree, where I don't, and where the framing is just missing something.

1. "Break into deterministic pieces" - this is workflow advice, not agentic AI advice.

The pipeline described at the conference - Transform, Route, Transform, Generate, Safety Check - is pre-defined steps with deterministic paths. That's workflow automation. It's not agentic AI.

They're different things. Agentic AI means the LLM decides which tool to run, when, and why. You can't pre-define that path without killing the intelligence. Your tools and skills should be deterministic. Your orchestration layer should not be. I've built this separation across three systems and the pattern holds every time. Non-determinism in the reasoning layer isn't the problem. It's the point.

2. "The blocker is leadership."

True. But there's a layer most people skip.

Leaders who haven't built anything themselves can't evaluate what they're being asked to approve. And leaders who treat governance as friction will keep producing slow pilots that go nowhere. Pedro URIA-RECIO, CDAO at CIMB, made this case at their Regional Data and AI Summit - governance isn't a brake. It's the infrastructure that lets AI actually scale. The organisations moving fastest are the ones where governance and building happen together, not one after the other. Delegation without understanding produces reports. Not outcomes.

3. "Ban DMs. Group channels only so AI has full context."

Context quantity isn't context quality.

Group channels are full of banter, irrelevant threads, and noise that has nothing to do with the work. Feed that to your AI and you don't get better reasoning... you get context rot. Diluted signal, wasted tokens, worse output. A well-curated input beats an unfiltered firehose every time. Context is a design problem. Not a channel policy.

4. On the recap itself.

"The org is becoming context for AI" is a sharp line. But it's surrounded by advice that most business leaders can't action. The practitioners in that room already know this stuff. The decision-makers who actually need to move aren't reading conference recaps.

5. The question nobody asked.

Not "how do we make AI more deterministic?" but "which layers should we control, and which should we stop trying to control?" Most organisations get this wrong before they even start building. That's the architecture decision that determines everything downstream.

#ArtificialIntelligence #AgenticAI #AIStrategy #AIAdoption #EnterpriseAI

text:
I asked OpenAI's Head of Codex whether we’re building the wrong parts of the future.

At AI Engineer Singapore, I got to ask Thibault Sottiaux something I’d been stuck on:

when something fails, do we fix it in the model, the harness, the skill, or somewhere else?

Because if we keep patching every model limitation with more infrastructure, we might accidentally build permanent systems around temporary weaknesses.

The rest of the weekend was just as wild.

I met Gavriel Cohen, creator of NanoClaw, and learnt more about what it takes to make autonomous coding agents secure.

Got to speak with Geoffrey Huntley, creator of the Ralph Loop, about software abundance… and then watched him DJ later that night. loved it.

Also still thinking about Dr. Vivian Balakrishnan’s point that we can outsource computation, memory, and knowledge retrieval, but not understanding or accountability.

AI is making it easier to build.
But it is not magically making us understand what we’re building.

Super grateful to have been one of the 20 student scholars selected for AI Engineer Singapore.

Huge thank you to AI Engineer and 65labs for making this possible.

fired up!

Last week was 🔥on ATP!! 

First, we had the pleasure of working with Salesforce to cover Agentforce World tour Singapore. 

Our biggest takeaway? Slackbot is probably a massive breakthrough. 

When you give an AI agent access to all internal communications that already happen on Slack, now the AI agents can be helpful at a whole new level. It can connect you with the internal stakeholders you need, or help perform tasks with all the information required - without any additional data setup, Slack itself becomes the data layer, and that is game changer. 

Thanks to the teams at RICE, A FINN Partners Company and Salesforce for helping us set this up! 

Then we went to AI Engineer Singapore, where we met with the people building the future of AI and the people building the AI ecosystem in Singapore. 

Our biggest takeaway was that 65labs is building something special there, they put Singapore on the global AI map thanks to the community they are building and the energy they are creating. Huge congrats to Rachael De Foe, Sherry Jiang and the rest of the team.

It’s beautiful to see so many people excited about AI, and working together to build the next generation of software and tools, and it was a pleasure to meet the community in person at these events! 

Thanks again to everyone who worked with us, and to all our amazing guests who came on the show. We will keep covering the most important tech stories in Asia with even more energy than ever thanks to these great events - see you at the next one! 🚀

A serving foreign minister, running his own AI agent off a three-year-old Raspberry Pi with 8GB of RAM. That's Vivian Balakrishnan at AI Engineer Singapore last week, explaining how he built a personal "second brain" with Claude over the last three months.

His reasoning was sharper than most enterprise AI strategy decks I've read. "You cannot govern a technology that you have only been briefed on." Get your hands dirty. Run the experiments yourself.

That principle scales beyond government. Anyone making AI decisions for a team, a function, or an enterprise builds sharper judgment once they have actually shipped something with the tools themselves, even something small.

Learning by doing is no longer optional for anyone responsible for the call.

text:
Had the chance last weekend to speak at the first AI Engineer Singapore conference about Lightsprint (YC P26)!

It really feels like the Singapore tech scene is catching a serious tailwind, fuelled by AI. The energy at the conference was proof of that — packed workshop rooms, a full main stage theatre, and three days of people showing up with genuine curiosity and momentum.

Huge thanks to Sherry Jiang and the rest of the 65labs team for putting together such a wonderful experience.

One thing that stood out to me: AI may be a centralizing force, but it is also a unifying one. I got to meet people from so many different communities I’ve been part of over the years. Engineering meetups, fintech, crypto, AI. old friends, new friends, and many people building at the intersections.

Excited for what’s ahead, and grateful for the chance to be part of Singapore tech’s next chapter.

text:
The moment I landed back in Singapore, I went straight to AI Engineer Singapore. 3 days of inspiration, excitement, and nonstop energy (literally slept for <1h on one of the days 🤣)

Every talk was about agents.
But every story still had a human at the center 💛

I volunteered at the Google DeepMind booth, where people were getting genuinely excited watching Nano Banana generate sticker packs of themselves on the spot. We watched people spin up vibe-coded projects on Google AI Studio and Antigravity straight from their phones. Engineers, designers, students, complete beginners… everyone was curious about the same tools.

In between shifts, I caught a bunch of talks too.

Gavriel Cohen spoke about autonomous agents reviewing every PR.
Sabina Cabrera shared her vision for a collaborative design workspace between humans and agents.
Justin Baird FRSA talked about embodied AI unlocking creative expression for people with disabilities.

Every talk kept returning to the same thing, agents, yes… but humans still very much at the heart of it all.

AI wasn’t framed as replacement. It was framed as expansion. Developers becoming designers. Disabled artists becoming creators. Small teams building at the speed of companies 100x their size. 

A little disruptive, definitely a little scary, but more so incredibly exciting.

What impressed me just as much was how the entire city showed up for this.
For the whole month, there were side events happening across Singapore almost every night, concurrently.

At Build with Cursor with Brian C., strangers openly shared their agentic workflows, e.g. how they switch between models, fine-tune open-source ones, go from Figma to production, manage context and doc, and so much more. 

People were genuinely trying to help each other build better!

Two years ago, I used to tell friends I couldn’t find the right community here. It felt like all the ambitious builders eventually left for San Francisco.

But something has clearly shifted.

Over the past few months, I’ve seen new communities popping up, more builders moving in, and events where people are actually shipping instead of just talking. For the first time in a while, it feels like Singapore might already be becoming that place.

So when 🥃 Agrim Singh said, “you are the scene,” that really resonated.

A scene isn’t a venue or a company.
It’s the people who keep showing up :)

Thank you to 65labs, 🥃 Agrim Singh, Sherry Jiang, Ivan Leo, 🇸🇬 Yong Quan Tan, Brian C. + rest of the crew, speakers, sponsors, volunteers for making this happen!

And to everyone who showed up, you’re the reason Singapore feel like the place to be right now ❤️

AIE recaps → https://lnkd.in/gBDtq5n5
Day 1 notes → https://lnkd.in/g6XchpMJ
Leadership recap → https://lnkd.in/g-vuZ8J8

text:
Why You Can’t Delegate Personal Understanding: Reflections on AI from Singapore’s Minister for Foreign Affairs, Dr. Vivian Balakrishnan.

I came across this fascinating keynote at the AI Engineer Singapore conference that challenged the traditional divide between policymakers and builders. 

Source -  https://lnkd.in/d6ciSA4J

Singapore’s Minister for Foreign Affairs, Dr. Vivian Balakrishnan, took the stage not just as a diplomat, but as a fellow tinkere and builder.

The Minister shared a powerful message for the AI era, The one thing which you cannot outsource is your personal understanding. While we can delegate computation and memory to machines, accountability and true understanding remain uniquely human.

Here are my top takeaways from his session:

1. Get Your Hands Dirty: Minister Vivian famously built his own second brain using NanoClaw, running on a Raspberry Pi with just 8GB of RAM. His toolkit includes WhatsApp for communication, Whisper for voice, and Obsidian for a personal cloud. His reasoning? You cannot govern a technology that you have only been briefed on.

2. Transformation Happens at the Individual Level: Real value isn't just created in massive data centers. The true payoff happens when ordinary peopleteachers, doctors, and even ministers use AI to re-engineer their own daily workflows.

Singapore’s Strategic Bet: While Singapore may not be at the absolute frontier of model development, the goal is to be at the frontier of deployment at scale. This requires a decentralized, ground-up approach where every citizen is empowered by these tools.

The barriers to entry have collapsed. It is no longer a question of Can we build this? but What should exist?.

As Minister Vivian put it: Learn by doing. Don't just read the headlines get your hands wet and start building the future today.

Learn by Doing - I've spent a year building my own AI system for training analytics, moving beyond using AI as just another tool to treating it as a strategic partner that guides my decision making. If you want to understand how to implement AI in your daily work not just prompt in any AI tool, but actually build systems that accelerate your business outcomes, comment SINGAPORE or DM me. Let's connect and discuss how you can transform AI from occasional use to systematic implementation that drives real results.

text:
Last week, I was really lucky to be one of the 20 students selected for a sponsored ticket to attend AI Engineer Singapore 2026. 

As someone who started building mainly out of curiosity, opportunities like this genuinely mean a lot to me. AI is moving so fast, and being able to learn directly from people who are actively shaping AI systems, products, and developer tools was something I really appreciated.

One thing that stuck with me was Dr Vivian Balakrishnan’s opening sharing: you cannot govern a technology you have only been briefed on. Seeing him as a minister, former surgeon, and builder himself reminded me that the best way to understand AI is to get hands-on, build, test, and learn by doing.

I also got to speak with Geoffrey Huntley, creator of the Ralph Loop, about software abundance and why we should try building our own coding agents, not just consume them. His point on removing waste from systems also stuck with me. Sometimes the bigger unlock is not adding more AI, but cutting the meetings, approvals, and friction that slow real work down. Watching him DJ later that night was also very cool.

Sara Hooker’s sharing also made me think a lot. She spoke about how the next phase of AI may be less about scaling bigger models and more about adaptability. As models get stronger, the bigger question is how well we can deploy them in real situations.

Ryo Lu from Cursor shared useful design tips that made me think more about how developer tools should feel simple, fast, and intuitive. I also liked the reminder that when you feel stuck, sometimes the best thing to do is to step away, take a walk, and clear the brain fog.

I also enjoyed Gabriel Chua’s OpenAI demo. It helped me understand Codex much better and how tools like this can be used in daily workflows to improve productivity.

It was also really nice meeting Bhavan Jaipragas, Deputy Opinion Editor at The Straits Times, and hearing his thoughts on the future of AI.

Had a great time with Max Buckley and Ishan Goswami at the Exa networking dinner, and also enjoyed speaking with Joseph Yang about his time at Cursor. He even let us try his Vibe-Coded typing test, which was fun.

Overall, I am very thankful for the whole experience. I got to learn a lot, meet people I would not usually get the chance to meet, and make new friends like Jesmine Goh, K Jagateesvaran Rajoo, and Aditya Arya.

Huge thank you to Rachael De Foe for making this opportunity possible and for supporting the student cohort throughout the conference. Also grateful to 65labs, Sherry Jiang, 🥃 Agrim Singh, and all the sponsors who made the student tickets possible.

I am especially grateful that they believed in bringing students into the space. Because of this, I got to experience first-hand how people at the frontier are thinking about AI, building with it, and shaping what comes next.

Truly grateful for this opportunity.

text:
my closing at AI Engineer singapore had these words on it: you are the scene.

we'd been hearing the opposite for years. on twitter, in DMs, from VCs who don't live here, from singaporeans who'd already left. "there's no AI scene in singapore." you hear it enough and you start to believe it. one of the reasons we ran AIE SG was honestly to find out if it was true.

turns out it isn't. but i didn't fully know that until i was on stage looking out at the crowd.

those last five minutes weren't really applause. the room was looking around at itself. people turning to the strangers next to them, clocking maybe for the first time that they weren't alone in this. nobody was going to arrive from somewhere else and validate them. it was already here, and had been here the whole time, and i think a lot of us hadn't quite let ourselves see it.

a student walked up to sarah hooker between sessions and asked her a question she said she'd never been asked. dr vivian balakrishnan showed up without an entourage and stayed longer than he needed to. a parent brought their kid to the conference. a sponsor pulled us aside afterward and said they should have done more. 

none of those are sizzle reel moments. 

they're what a room looks like when the people in it actually wanted to be there. this is what an actual high-signal event means.

we made specific choices to make this a no bullshit affair. a 10,000-person conference can give you a name tag and a brand impression but it can't give you a real conversation. 

we kept the room small enough that people would actually collide. 

we flew 90% of the speakers in rather than filling the lineup recycling the same 10 people who speak at all conferences in south-east asia. 

we built the program around people shipping right now who have opinions about where this is going, not people doing thought leadership laps. 

we got everyone to get their hands dirty - no point talking shop if you've never used the tools. 

we said no to a lot this year, and we're planning to keep saying no. this is what helps curate the BEST experience. singapore deserves the best.

we built the whole thing in 90 days but spent much longer validating this through the singapore community with 65labs. the demand has been there for over a year. we just needed to put it in one place at one time so it could see itself.

i think about this a lot now. it wasn't really a conference - it was a mirror.

to Sherry Jiang Rachael De Foe Kaspar Hidayat Adlin Zainal Ivan Leo Nehal Agrawal 🇸🇬 Yong Quan Tan. to Brian C. Daren T. and the volunteers who didn't sleep. to the sponsors who sent researchers and builders instead of BD. to the speakers who flew in for this and only this. thank you.

and to everyone who was in the room: you don't need permission for any of this. you didn't need it before this week, you don't need it now. there isn't a scene out there waiting to invite you in. you already are it. 

see you at AIE SG 2027

we made specific choices to make this a no bullshit affair. a 10,000-person conference can give you a name tag and a brand impression but it can't give you a real conversation. 

we kept the room small enough that people would actually collide. 

we flew 90% of the speakers in rather than filling the lineup recycling the same 10 people who speak at all conferences in south-east asia. 

we built the program around people shipping right now who have opinions about where this is going, not people doing thought leadership laps. 

we got everyone to get their hands dirty - no point talking shop if you've never used the tools. 

we said no to a lot this year, and we're planning to keep saying no. this is what helps curate the BEST experience. singapore deserves the best.

we built the whole thing in 90 days but spent much longer validating this through the singapore community with 65labs. the demand has been there for over a year. we just needed to put it in one place at one time so it could see itself.

i think about this a lot now. it wasn't really a conference - it was a mirror.

to Sherry Jiang Rachael De Foe Kaspar Hidayat Adlin Zainal Ivan Leo Nehal Agrawal 🇸🇬 Yong Quan Tan. to Brian C. Daren T. and the volunteers who didn't sleep. to the sponsors who sent researchers and builders instead of BD. to the speakers who flew in for this and only this. thank you.

and to everyone who was in the room: you don't need permission for any of this. you didn't need it before this week, you don't need it now. there isn't a scene out there waiting to invite you in. you already are it. 

see you at AIE SG 2027

text:
Three days. A single conference. A completely different perspective on where AI is headed. 🇸🇬

I was at the very first 𝗔𝗜 𝗘𝗻𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗲𝗲𝗿 𝗦𝘂𝗺𝗺𝗶𝘁 𝗦𝗶𝗻𝗴𝗮𝗽𝗼𝗿𝗲 and frankly it was an eye-opener. It's not just about what AI can do at work, but how it's quietly changing the way we live.

Some moments that stood out:
𝗗𝗮𝘆 𝟭 – 𝗪𝗼𝗿𝗸𝘀𝗵𝗼𝗽. Gotta get my hands dirty on EXA AI for research agents, Convex for reliable AI apps, OpenAI's Codex, PostHog's closed-loop product engine and AI research agents. Real builders, real code, real talk.

𝗗𝗮𝘆𝘀 𝟮 & 𝟯 – 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗯𝗶𝗴 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗴𝗲. Leaders from across the AI ecosystem - startups and enterprise – sharing what's working, what's not and what's coming up. I was especially struck by the Physical AI showcase, where assistive robotics is really helping people with disabilities build confidence and independence. Best of humane technology.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗸𝗲𝘆𝗻𝗼𝘁𝗲 𝗜 𝘄𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝗮𝗹𝘄𝗮𝘆𝘀 𝗿𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗺𝗯𝗲𝗿. Dr Vivian Balakrishnan, Singapore's Minister for Foreign Affairs, started us off with "Building a 'Second Brain'". He's running his own AI system on a Raspberry Pi with 8GB of RAM – using open source tools and a pinch of stubborn curiosity. A Foreign Minister standing on stage, talking like a builder. Only in Singapore.

Three days in and I'm leaving with more questions than answers — which is exactly how a good conference should feel. Huge thanks to the team behind AIE Singapore. See you in the next summit.
#AIEngineerSummit #AIESingapore  #AIAgents

text:
Singapore's Foreign Minister stood on stage last week and told the room his most-used AI tool runs on a Raspberry Pi.

A 2 to 3 year old one. 8GB of RAM. Sitting on his desk.

That little box runs his personal AI agent. He calls it NanoClaw. He uses it every day — to prep for meetings, draft speeches, recall facts from a hundred conversations across 12 countries in a month.

He built it himself.

Dr Vivian Balakrishnan spoke at AI Engineer Singapore on 16 May. He opened by calling himself a "retired eye surgeon" who likes to tinker. Then he walked the room through his stack — NanoClaw, Ollama, whisper.cpp, mnemon, Obsidian. Open source parts, assembled by hand over three months.

One line from his speech keeps coming back to me:

"𝗬𝗼𝘂 𝗰𝗮𝗻𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗴𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗻 𝗮 𝘁𝗲𝗰𝗵𝗻𝗼𝗹𝗼𝗴𝘆 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗵𝗮𝘃𝗲 𝗼𝗻𝗹𝘆 𝗯𝗲𝗲𝗻 𝗯𝗿𝗶𝗲𝗳𝗲𝗱 𝗼𝗻."

And another one:

"𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘄𝗵𝗶𝗰𝗵 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗰𝗮𝗻𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗼𝘂𝘁𝘀𝗼𝘂𝗿𝗰𝗲 𝗶𝘀 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗽𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗹 𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗿𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴."

Read those again. Slowly.

This is a sitting Minister. He could have any team build anything for him. Instead, he chose to get his own hands dirty. Not to look clever. Because he believes you cannot lead on something you haven't touched.

That is rare. That is humility. That is what serious leadership looks like.

Thank you, Sir. For the lesson. And for showing what curiosity looks like at the top.


#AI #SingaporeTech #TechLeadership #AIEngineer

"𝗬𝗼𝘂 𝗰𝗮𝗻𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗴𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗻 𝗮 𝘁𝗲𝗰𝗵𝗻𝗼𝗹𝗼𝗴𝘆 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗵𝗮𝘃𝗲 𝗼𝗻𝗹𝘆 𝗯𝗲𝗲𝗻 𝗯𝗿𝗶𝗲𝗳𝗲𝗱 𝗼𝗻."

And another one:

"𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘄𝗵𝗶𝗰𝗵 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗰𝗮𝗻𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗼𝘂𝘁𝘀𝗼𝘂𝗿𝗰𝗲 𝗶𝘀 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗽𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗹 𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗿𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴."

Read those again. Slowly.

This is a sitting Minister. He could have any team build anything for him. Instead, he chose to get his own hands dirty. Not to look clever. Because he believes you cannot lead on something you haven't touched.

That is rare. That is humility. That is what serious leadership looks like.

Thank you, Sir. For the lesson. And for showing what curiosity looks like at the top.

text:
From Raspberry Pie (food tech) to Raspberry Pi:
If AI Engineer Singapore 2026 showcased the energy and enthusiasm of builders in the AI community, AI Student Developer Conference 2026 highlighted that guardrails are needed to ensure AI is deployed responsibly and meaningfully.
Some key takeaways from the sessions:
• The first panel on digital trust and security reinforced that topics around data governance, compliance, transparency, and trust are just as important as model performance itself.
• The second panel on AI for science emphasized the growing importance of being “bilingual”, which is combining deep domain expertise with AI and coding skills. The professors termed it: ‘double-edged sword’.
• Domain knowledge remains the key differentiator. AI can amplify expertise, but it cannot replace fundamental understanding. Build things up from first principles.

Edge computing was a foreign concept to me, but I feel that it is something interesting to tinker with. Overall, the event was a good reminder that the future of AI is not just about building smarter systems, but also about building systems that are trustworthy, governed responsibly, and grounded in real-world expertise.

text:
✨𝗚𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗳𝘂𝗹 𝘁𝗼 𝗵𝗮𝘃𝗲 𝗯𝗲𝗲𝗻 𝗽𝗮𝗿𝘁 𝗼𝗳 𝗔𝗜 𝗘𝗻𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗲𝗲𝗿 𝗦𝗶𝗻𝗴𝗮𝗽𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝟮𝟬𝟮𝟲✨

A week ago, I wasn't even supposed to be there. Hong Bing Sim jio-ed me and 3 other Malaysians to volunteer Bede Lau Heng Yi Kang Lavanesswary Lavanesswary (and Olivia Lim Yun Xuan). I travel to SG often with other Malaysians for events; but AI Engineer? No way. L̶a̶s̶t̶-̶m̶i̶n̶u̶t̶e̶ application, l̶a̶s̶t̶-̶m̶i̶n̶u̶t̶e̶ acceptance, m̶i̶d̶n̶i̶g̶h̶t̶ ̶b̶u̶s̶ to Singapore, l̶a̶s̶t̶-̶m̶i̶n̶u̶t̶e̶ accommodation crashed at a friend's place (lifesaver – otherwise it would've been a campus bench again). We couldn't afford the AIE tickets, but we could volunteer to be in the room. 𝘚𝘰 𝘸𝘦 𝘵𝘰𝘰𝘬 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘭𝘦𝘢𝘱.

Three days of being on our feet, sleep-deprived. Pretty sure we cleared Singapore's 10,000-steps-a-day target every single day. Saturday May 16 was the worst – 𝕡𝕠𝕦𝕣𝕚𝕟𝕘 𝕣𝕒𝕚𝕟, and a big chunk of my shift was guiding attendees between Capitol Theatre and Pullman, running umbrellas out to people stuck in the downpour.

But it was still one of the most meaningful weekends I've had in a while. I left with a sharper mental model of 𝘸𝘩𝘦𝘳𝘦 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘧𝘪𝘦𝘭𝘥 𝘪𝘴 𝘢𝘤𝘵𝘶𝘢𝘭𝘭𝘺 𝘮𝘰𝘷𝘪𝘯𝘨. A few takeaways stuck with me:

→ The bottleneck has moved from the model to the harness. Vivian Balakrishnan (yes, Singapore's Foreign Minister – who walked past me within inches) is running his diplomatic prep on an 8GB Raspberry Pi with NanoClaw + a graph memory system + Obsidian. His line: "tools matter more than models."

→ Verification is the new bottleneck, not generation. Stripe runs 3,000 PRs/week through internal "Minions" agents at a 65% one-shot merge rate – and the secret sauce is an LLM judge that only sees the original prompt + current diff, so the worker agent can't talk it into "done."

→ The economics of software have flipped. Geoffrey Huntley's line: "software development now costs less than minimum wage." Max Buckley from Exa put it sharper – code commoditizes, brand and distribution become the moat.

→ Singapore is genuinely emerging as an APAC AI operating hub. GovTech Singapore is building a sovereign agentic harness for 150k public officers.

The other thing I'm taking home is the operational craft of pulling off something like this. 1,000+ paid attendees, multiple venues, workshops + main stage + exhibitions running in parallel, in the rain, with a last-minute scholarship program when a sponsor pulled out two days before launch. Volunteer lead Brian C. calmly redirected chaos in real time. Sherry Jiang, 🥃 Agrim Singh, Kaspar Hidayat, Rachael De Foe and the 65labs team held the whole thing together. 𝓉𝒽𝒶𝓃𝓀 𝓎ℴ𝓊 for trusting last-minute Malaysian volunteers and making us feel like we belonged.

To Malaysians who want to travel to Singapore together for AI events like this, DM me and I'll add you into the family.

Already locked in for AIE SG 2027 🇸🇬

#AIEngineer #AIEngineerSingapore #65Labs #Singapore #AI

authorMeta.headline: strat comms for tech founders • ai engineer singapore (15-17 may)

text:
A full page in the newspaper about AI Engineer Singapore!!

The funny thing is… I don’t fully agree with what the Straits Times ran.

The better thing is… I love that I don’t.

What mattered more were the moments that led to the article: 

👉On Day 1 of AIE, we held a workshop for journalists to try building with tools like Codex for the first time. I met Bhavan irl, got to show him some of my own workflows, and build a few ideas together.

(Being next to someone for their first real “whoa, what?!” moment never gets old.)

👉👉On Day 2, he sat through talks that showed the range of what AI’s frontier looks like now. 

A stage that didn’t only have folks from Silicon Valley but was shared by builders from Singapore… including our Foreign Minister Dr Vivian Balakrishnan, Ego AI’s founder (and ACS alumnus) Vishnu H. and more. (All mentioned in the article too!)

👉👉👉On Day 3, some of the sponsored students heard Bhavan was attending and asked to meet him. 

They were excited that a newsroom had shown up to understand builders up close.
They genuinely wanted to hear what he thought.
They also wanted share their own hopes, questions, and worries too.

I don’t agree with everything in the article. (Some parts I do) But mostly, I appreciated that he stepped into the space and made sense of it for himself.

Funny enough, the team’s first reaction was surprise at being called “tech elite”. Most of us still feel like gremlins hauling boxes of pizza and swag around Singapore, doing our best to make things work.

But maybe that reaction says something important too?

In AI, it’s easy to feel frustrated when people “don’t get it.” But most people never get the chance to step close enough to feel the shift for themselves.

That’s why the 65Labs team works so damn hard to leave the door open.

Technical or not, we want this ecosystem to feel like one that anyone can step into, question, explore, and shape… as long as they’re curious enough to try.

Thank you Bhavan Jaipragas for saying yes to coming down, and for showing others in Singapore that our invitation remains open.

Not everyone needs to agree on AI’s future.

But everyone deserves the chance to try building it for themselves.

—-
Sherry Jiang 🥃 Agrim Singh Adlin Zainal Nehal Agrawal 🇸🇬 Yong Quan Tan Brian C. Ivan Leo Kaspar Hidayat Daren T.
